newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe won't waive secrecy in French bugging probe.
newsitem.headline: Juppe won't waive secrecy in French bugging probe.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe has refused to lift official secrecy to allow defendants in an investigation into illegal wire-tapping under the late president Francois Mitterrand to prepare their defence, his office said on Friday.

Gilles Menage, who headed Mitterrand's private office in the early 1980s, wrote to Juppe last month asking for secrecy to be lifted so he could defend himself against charges of invasion of privacy "in equitable conditions".
Menage has contended that all the wiretaps were justified on national security grounds.

"The prime minister replied on March 17 that he was unable to grant this request, consistent with the position taken by his predecessor in response a similar request by the judge," Juppe's press service said.
It said the decision was in line with long-standing jurisprudence upheld by civil courts and the Council of State, France's highest administrative court.

Secret files from Mitterrand's anti-terrorist unit, published by the media on Thursday, showed the Socialist president personally ordered widespread telephone-tapping to protect his private life and spy on lawyers and journalists.

The disclosure drew angry editorials but virtually no comment from the Socialist party, now in opposition, or the ruling centre-right coalition, leading to speculation that phone-tapping is still common.
But one parliamentarian demanded that the head of state should be made liable to criminal investigation.

Patrick Devedjian, a deputy for President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, told the daily Le Monde that the head of state "cannot be investigated, save for cases of 'high treason' which no text defines."
"The president is therefore above the law," he said. "This situation therefore poses a problem even beyond Francois Mitterrand's behaviour."
Le Monde and the magazine L'Express published what they said were extracts from files seized by DST counter-espionage officers and investigating magistrates in February.

The archives, stored in a garage outside Paris rented by the unit's former head, Christian Prouteau, included recordings of telephone-taps, demands for presidential favours and memos on terrorism suspects.
Both reports said many notes destined for Mitterrand carried his laconic handwritten comment: "Vu" (Seen).
"The Fifth Republic is a monarchical, albeit republican system in which the president does not follow common rules," said Le Monde journalist Edwy Plenel.

Plenel, whose phone was tapped when he investigated the sinking of the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior by the French secret service in 1985, added: "I would like to be certain that practices do not continue today."
Investigating magistrate Jean-Paul Valat questioned Prouteau, who invoked official secrets rules, for eight hours on Thursday.

Prouteau, two former senior government officials and three members of the now-disbanded unit are under investigation over the alleged telephone tapping of dozens of politicians, writers, lawyers and journalists without judicial permission.

The supreme court last month rejected a bid to stop the investigation, ruling that the statute of limitations in invasion of privacy cases applied only from the moment the offence was discovered, not the date when it was committed.
